name: Candomblé
info: Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion that developed in Brazil during the 19th century, mainly in Bahia, from West and Central African religions and Roman Catholicism, and is known for its orixás, its terreiros and its ritual of possession.

facts.origin: Brazil, mainly the Bahia region, in the 19th century, among Afro-Brazilian communities formed under the Atlantic slave trade; by the founding myth the first terreiro, the Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká, was founded in Salvador in 1830.
facts.founder: none: the religion arose through the blending of Yoruba, Fon and Bantu religions with Roman Catholicism, and it has no central authority; each terreiro is autonomous under its own mãe or pai de santo.
facts.scriptures: none: Candomblé has no central sacred text. Its knowledge, the fundamentos, is passed on in the terreiros, and divination draws on odu, mythological stories linked to the patterns of cowrie shells.
facts.followers: One census report indicated that around 1.3 percent of Brazil's population identified as followers, a figure likely to reflect only initiates; a 1997 census recorded 1,144 terreiros in Salvador.

t: Candomblé venerates spirits called orixás, inkice or vodun, who are held to be subservient to a distant creator god, Olodumaré, and each person is believed to have a tutelary orixá who informs their personality.

It has no central authority or sacred text: it is organised around autonomous terreiros led by a mãe or pai de santo, and divided into nations, of which the Ketu, Jeje and Angola are the most prominent.

Its practitioners drum, sing and dance so that an orixá may possess one of them, and the religion has met discrimination, being labelled devil worship by some critics and attacked by Evangelical opponents in the 2000s.
dyk: Every initiate is given a new name, the nome de santo, which usually indicates the identity of their tutelary orixá, and receives a string of beads coloured for that orixá: white for Oxalá, dark blue for Ogum, red and white for Xangô.
ev: Enslaved Africans first arrive in Brazil
By the founding myth of Candomblé, the Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká, from which the Nagô tradition descends, is founded in Salvador as the first terreiro
Brazil emancipates all slaves, having abolished the slave trade in 1850
The republican constitution enshrines freedom of religion, although the Penal Code of 1890 had prohibited Spiritism, talismans and much herbal medicine
Candomblé becomes increasingly public, and Law Decree 1202 under President Getúlio Vargas recognises the legitimacy of terreiros
Brazilians take part in the first International Congress of Orisha Tradition and Culture in Ifẹ, Nigeria
Evangelical Protestant opposition grows, including physical attacks on practitioners and terreiros, and Candomblecistas respond with protest marches

sections.origins:
Candomblé is an African diasporic religion that developed in Brazil during the 19th century. It arose from the blending of the traditional religions that enslaved West and Central Africans, mostly Yoruba, Fon and Bantu, brought with them and the Roman Catholicism of the Portuguese colonialists. Enslaved Africans first arrived in Brazil in the 1530s. They came at first largely from the Guinea coast, by the 17th century mostly from Angola and Congo, and between 1775 and 1850 mostly Yoruba and Dahomean from the Gulf of Benin. Around four million Africans were transported to Brazil, more than to any other part of the Americas, and they were concentrated predominantly in Bahia.

On arrival the enslaved were divided into “nations” largely by port of embarkation, so that Africans of different cultural backgrounds were grouped under one name; those from the Bight of Benin were called “Nagô”. As the Yoruba and Dahomean people made up the last wave, their cosmology became ascendant. Of the thousands of orishas venerated in West Africa, far fewer continued to be worshipped in Brazil, and those associated with agriculture were abandoned, as slaves had little reason to protect the harvests of slave-owners. By the 18th century African-derived rituals were commonly reported and were called calundu, a term of Bantu origin.

The earliest terreiros appeared in Bahia in the early 19th century. According to what the scholar Stefania Capone called “the founding myth of Candomblé”, the first was the Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká, also known as the Casa Branca or Engenho Velho, founded in Salvador in 1830, from which the Nagô tradition descends.
sections.beliefs:
Candomblé teaches the existence of a supreme divinity called Olorun or Olodumare, regarded as the creator of everything but thought distant and unapproachable, and so not specifically worshipped. The religion revolves around spirits termed orixás or santos, called inkice in the Angola tradition and vodun in the Jeje tradition. Believed to mediate between humanity and Olorun, they are conceived variously as ancestral figures or as embodiments of forces of nature, and each is associated with particular colours, foods and animals. Oxalá is the chief orixá, Xangô is associated with thunder, Ogum with battle and iron, Iemanjá with the ocean, and Exú, a trickster, is honoured and fed first because he guards entrances. Each orixá is equated with a Roman Catholic saint, and Ogum, for instance, with St Anthony of Padua.

Practitioners believe that everyone is linked to a tutelary orixá, the dono da cabeça, or master of the head, who informs their personality and whose identity is ascertained through divination. Candomblé also teaches of axé, a force described by scholars as the spiritual force of the universe, which can concentrate in leaves, roots and blood. Beside the orixás stand the exus, which are held to be capable of both good and bad acts, the caboclos, spirits typically of indigenous Americans or backwoodsmen, and the eguns, the spirits of the dead.

Candomblé generally has no fixed ethical precepts. It stresses equilibrium between competing forces rather than a dichotomy of good and evil, and problems are often read as disharmony with one’s orixá. Each year has a festival cycle that runs from the feast of Oxalá in September to that of Iemanjá in February.
sections.texts:
Candomblé has no central sacred text and no central authority to determine doctrine and orthodoxy. It is heterogeneous, with regional variation in belief and practice, and each lineage or community approaches the religion in ways informed by its tradition and the choices of its leader. Its knowledge is called the fundamentos, the “foundations”, and is guarded by practitioners; the scholar Paul Johnson has characterised the religion, which makes use of secrecy, as a secret society. African-derived words are used in ritual: those of Yoruba origin predominate in the Nagô nation, those from Ewe-Fon languages in the Jeje nations and words from the Bantu languages in the Angola nation.

Mythological stories called odu are associated with each configuration of the cowrie shells used in the most common form of divination, the dilogun or jogo dos buzios, in which sixteen shells are commonly thrown. Healing and good conduct are likewise tied to lessons imparted in mythological tales. Yoruba divination by Ifá was characterised by the start of the 21st century as either extinct or very rare in Brazil.

Writing about Candomblé has shaped the religion itself. The 1930s saw a proliferation of academic studies by scholars such as Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, Edison Carneiro and Ruth Landes, most focusing on the Nagô tradition, and this literature, both scholarly and popular, helped document Candomblé while contributing to its standardisation. Many terreiros own copies of academic studies, sometimes to convey an image of authority.
sections.spread:
Candomblé coalesced primarily in the Bahia region in the 19th century. The late 19th century saw the first terreiros open in Rio de Janeiro, a city then expanding rapidly, and various upper-class white Brazilians began seeking out the religion. In the 20th century growing emigration from Bahia spread Candomblé throughout Brazil and abroad. Growing Afro-Brazilian migration to São Paulo brought a rapid rise there: from virtually no terreiros until the 1960s, the city had over 4000 by the century’s end. Candomblé also influenced the development of another religion, Umbanda, in the 1920s.

It is centred largely in and around Salvador, sometimes called “Black Rome” and regarded by some followers as a holy city, and practitioners in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo often regard Bahian terreiros as more authentic. Smaller communities exist elsewhere in South America, including Argentina and Uruguay, and in European countries such as Portugal, Spain, France, Belgium, Germany and Italy. Outside Brazil practitioners have faced challenges in performing animal sacrifice, which Germany, for instance, bans by law. Growing links were established with other African diasporic and West African religions, and Brazilians attended the first International Congress of Orisha Tradition and Culture in Ifẹ, Nigeria, in 1981; the second was held in Salvador in 1983.

Both in Brazil and abroad the religion has spread beyond its Afro-Brazilian origins and is practised by people of various ethnicities.
sections.community:
Candomblé is organised around terreiros, also called ilês, each of them independent and autonomous. A priestess who runs a terreiro is a mãe de santo, and a priest a pai de santo; in Nagô Candomblé these are an iyalorixá and a babalorixá. They educate novices, adjudicate disputes and provide healing and divination, often as their main income, and a terreiro will often disband when its chief priest or priestess dies. Most terreiros in Bahia are led by women, and the religion has been called female-dominated, with scholarly debate on whether it can be labelled matriarchal. The community of a terreiro is called an egbé and is regarded as a family. An initiate of seven years may undergo the deká ceremony, be regarded as an ebomi and open their own terreiro.

Candomblé is initiatory. Initiation, called fazer cabeça, “to make the head”, is usually very expensive, lasts from a few weeks to a few months and includes seclusion, the giving of a saint’s name and the seating of the orixá. Most Candomblecistas also practise Roman Catholicism. Candomblé divides into nations, the most prominent being the Nagô or Ketu, the Jeje and the Angola; the Nagô is the largest, and an initiate can change nation, called “changing the waters”.

Followers are called povo de santo, “people of saint”, or Candomblecistas. In Brazil the religion is largely urban and found among the poor, with most followers being Black women, while membership is more diverse in the south.
sections.legacy:
Brazil’s constitution of 1891 enshrined freedom of religion, yet Candomblé remained marginalised by the Roman Catholic establishment, which typically associated it with criminality, and the Penal Code of 1890 prohibited Spiritism, talismans and much herbal medicine. Authorities shut down terreiros, claiming they were a threat to public health. In the 1930s Law Decree 1202 recognised the legitimacy of terreiros and the Penal Code of 1940 offered them additional protections. Practitioners have encountered intolerance and discrimination: the label macumba, associated with sorcery, is applied to the religion, and more hostile views regard it as devil worship. Roman Catholics hold mixed opinions, while Evangelical and Pentecostal groups more uniformly target Candomblecistas as part of a “spiritual war” against Satan. The 2000s saw growing Evangelical opposition, including physical attacks on practitioners and terreiros, to which Candomblecistas responded with protest marches.

By the late 20th century Candomblé was increasingly respectable, and tourist literature later portrayed it as an intrinsic part of Brazilian culture. It has been seen as a treasured symbol of Brazilian cultural identity and an icon of African Diaspora culture and politics. Some practitioners, notably Mãe Stella Azevedo, have sought to “re-Africanise” the religion by removing Roman Catholic elements, while others reject this. It features in films, in the novels of Jorge Amado and Toni Morrison and in Brazilian popular music, and the bedroom of the priestess Mãe Menininha do Gantois was recognised as a heritage site in 2002.

summary: Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion that took shape in 19th-century Bahia, when enslaved Yoruba, Fon and Bantu religious traditions met Roman Catholicism. Its autonomous terreiros venerate orixás through drumming, dance and possession. Long marginalised and often attacked, it is now also seen as a symbol of Brazilian cultural identity.
references: Stefania Capone, Searching for Africa in Brazil: Power and Tradition in Candomblé (Duke University Press, 2010)
Paul Christopher Johnson, Secrets, Gossip, and Gods: The Transformation of Brazilian Candomblé (Oxford University Press, 2002)
James Lorand Matory, Black Atlantic Religion: Tradition, Transnationalism, and Matriarchy in the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé (Princeton University Press, 2005)
Luis Nicolau Parés, The Formation of Candomblé: Vodun History and Ritual in Brazil (University of North Carolina Press, 2013)
notes: Start 1830 (circa): the article says only that Candomblé developed in the 19th century, with the earliest terreiros in the early 19th century; 1830 is the date of the first terreiro by what Capone calls the founding myth.
Left out as restricted or graphic: the detail of initiation cuts, which the article gives; the fundamentos are said to be guarded. Only a brief mention of seclusion and the saint's name is made.
The article contradicts itself on Ifá: Oxum is married to Ifa as orixá of divination, while later Ifá is a Yoruba divinatory system said to be rare in Brazil. Only the second is used.
The article writes 'Olorun or Olodumare'; the lead gives Olodumaré. The profile uses Olorun or Olodumare.
Both 'Oxalá/Oxala', 'Exú/Exu' and 'Ogum/Ogun' spellings occur in the article; Portuguese forms used.
'Most followers being black women' is rendered 'Black women'. 'Ebomi' is described twice in the article with different wording; the deká after seven years is used.
